last_seal.decision: Own mix, between risk parity and the formula: L13 0.25, L11 0.12, L12 0.12, L16 0.12, L10 0.10, L5 0.08, L17 0.08, L1 0.07, L9 0.06. Main reason: with five noisy live days and a caution that every simple rule beat the formula on past data, I spread the book over nine sleeves, tilt toward low volatility and non-negative unflattered backtests, halve or more the formula's concentrated bets on L10 and L17, hold nothing in breaker, and keep the book close to market-neutral rather than betting on either continuation or rebound.
last_seal.bull: L13 Pairs reversion earns the full 25%: lowest volatility in the book (0.10% a day), a positive unflattered backtest and a small gain through a week in which SPY lost 8.6%. L11 SPY overnight, L12 Turn of month and L9 Sector rotation have the three best unflattered backtest averages (+0.055, +0.073, +0.050% a day), yet the formula gives L11 and L9 nothing; they deserve a share. L5 RSI(2) pullback is the one sleeve built to buy after a week like this one and its backtest is not negative. L16 SPY trend short is the only sleeve that has paid in this regime (+8.8% in five days, positive over 20 and 60 days) and is the natural offset to the long sleeves.
last_seal.bear: Five live days in a single one-directional selloff say almost nothing: L16, L14 and L15 look brilliant and L6, L8, L9 terrible for the same reason, and a sharp rebound from VIX 36 would flip all of it. L16's backtest average is negative, so its live gain is regime luck, not an edge. The formula's 25% in L10 rests on a flattered, negative backtest and a sleeve that did not trade at all this week, and its 25% in L17 backs a sleeve that has lost over 5, 20 and 60 days; low volatility is not the same as an edge. L1's low volatility also hides a negative backtest. Even the positive backtest averages are a few hundredths of a percent a day over 120 days, well within noise.

montecarlo.method: block bootstrap, 10000 paths, blocks of 5 days, seed 20261121; shared draws across series

replay.caveat: past data replayed with the allocator's rules; survivorship and hindsight flatter it

crash_drill.limits:
- Daily sleeves only (L5-L13, L15, L16, and L17 where its ETFs have archive history). The intraday sleeves (L1-L4,
  L14), baseline A, the options tracks and the crypto tracks have no data that far back and are absent.
- The stock list is today's S&P 100, so companies that fell out of the index before today are missing (survivorship
  bias). That flatters every stock-picking sleeve; the true result would be worse.
- Regime labels use the archive's SPY and VIX; costs are today's cost model.
The result is a stress reading of the allocation rules, not evidence that the strategies work.

rows.strategy: Agent picks: smart calls (delta 0.6, 7-21d, no earnings)

engine_vs_lag.note: measurement only: fills.py keeps using engine prices for baseline rows detected within 20 minutes; a mean cost clearly above 0 over 100+ rows would mean the engine fill is harsher than the 5-minute rule, a mean below 0 that it flatters

slippage.note: spread = what a market order pays now; drift = price move between the simulated fill and the quote (mostly the hourly-run delay); the simulation charges model_side_cost per side

a1.rule: Quantavius's weekly book vs the foundation-only equal weight; PASS at P >= 0.9 with a higher Sharpe

g1_rank.rule: daily ranking of 44 stocks, Spearman IC; 60 sealed days, P >= 0.9

g1_picks.rule: picks open to close vs the random control list; 60 pick days, P >= 0.9

g2.rule: approved lab strategies, forward trades only (AS sleeve)
